currently node acs servers are located in us oregon we need to document the impact of physical distance to server performance to our customers it is not always possible to have node acs server running close to the source or majority clients nodejs however this is a common problem and there are some ways to improve performance but should be considered app by app efficiently use cache caching data inside node acs server in memory without having to lookup the source and build on the fly every time could significantly improve overall app performance reduce response data size from node acs to client always use compression and send back only essential data set if possible to improve mobile app performance it is recommended to have one api call to get minimum set data synchronously to display on the device another async api call to load additional data consider using s or cloudfront for large data if node acs aggregates large set of data and the data doesn t change all the time it would be a good idea to upload them to s or cloudfront and have the client download the data from s or cloudfront instead so the client would make an api call to node acs server to get the url to the s or cloudfront data then the client can make another api call to s or cloudfront to download the real data it is never recommended to have node acs directly transfer large amount of data to the client use cloudfront to store static contents it is strongly discouraged to keep static content inside a node acs app if developers can move all static contents to cloudfront ahead of time then they would see big performance in their node acs app in principle node acs app should be only used to provide dynamic data heroku has a section talking about how to use amazon cloudfront it is probably a good idea to have a section in our node acs guide as well

developers would like to have information like this message from jeff included in the guides this is a common misconception about how this all works and it s mysterious because it s also complicated so let me clear up and explain a few things first off each platform implementation has the need to be slightly different although the goal is to make that a hidden issue from you the developer so all of my statements below have a ton of caveats here and there i m going to explain as best i can titanium is not single threaded it s multi threaded however like all ui based systems both legacy and modern it s single thread from the point of view of rendering all rendering and any related ui api calls are single threaded across the entire app this is how the browser works objective c java swing flash you name it all ui rendering is done on the main thread regardless of how many application threads you can create in native code and no matter how massively parallel you attempt to do other things at some point you ll need to render something and that will need to happen on one thread typically called the ui thread or the main thread in most ui systems each titanium context i e the main app js or in the case of a multi context app that uses a different url to open a window is a native thread it s not the main ui thread all cpu operations against all apis run within this context thread we call this a krollcontext in titanium native framework code so at the least you will always have threads the application thread and the main ui thread there are many caveats but some apis also create their own thread as well on top of that the most common example is the networking api such as xhr if you create an xhr request it will happen on a different thread however any operations against the app will then be executed back on the app thread and any ui operations will then happen on the main ui thread settimeout setinterval don t happen on a separate thread they are simply timers one is a one time the other is a repeatable timer that when activated will execute the js logic back on the context thread so using settimeout setinterval doesn t give you anything more than a timing function sometimes this can actually be useful in the case you want to do something on a later cycle of the cpu much like the nexttick on node however trying to get multi threaded behavior from it is futile it won t work what we probably need to do is separate out ui performance rendering from application api code execution performance since they seem related but are entirely unrelated in real terms from a code and performance optimization standpoint if there are ui performance rendering issues or bottlenecks we have two typical solutions re work the app to optimize it we often find simple app optimizations issues or structure issues to help fix that or we have a performance bottleneck in the native code or some use case that we have dealt with or optimized for and need to optimize the code or come up with a different api for the use case for the api code execution there is always better native code generation or framework improvements we are constantly making as we find bottle necks in fact there are two internal projects right now that are focused around giving us some better capabilities and in particular performance optimization improvements is around building a ground up ast parser that we ll be able to use in many different projects but one is around code optimization dead code elimination path analysis etc and a new app framework that will include an ability to compile code in to the native ui optimized formats at build time such as a xib for ios or android layout xml those are things that are always on going in the product and are with an eye towards constant speed improvements there might be another thing we need to support probably first through a module that i have heard many different use cases for and that s a worker pool often when i hear people trying to create parallel or separately executable pieces of code i e traditional multi threading use cases i believe most of these use cases might be solved if we had a concept of a worker pool much like the emerging web worker in html this could give app developers a simpler way to create pools of background tasks that can be easily managed but still had the underlying complexity of how the native threading works however even in web workers on the web you re still going to always be limited at some point by the ui rendering itself the best way for us to tackle these issues is to really get concrete around specific use cases and standalone app projects that we can look at the code see the results under the profiler and determine where the real issues are with the performance if you have specific issues the best way is to create a standalone app project zip it up and try and create a jira around what you re seeing then post it here to give us an additional heads up we can t immediately solve all issues but we certainly need specific examples to be able to address them and be confident we re actually solving the right problems
